edges.effect_quant: The clearest signal is a lower incidence of myopia when children spend substantially more time outdoors, with both trial and cohort data pointing the same way.
edges.mechanism: Outdoor light exposure appears to slow the refractive drift toward myopia through retinal dopamine signaling and reduced hyperopic defocus during near-work-heavy childhood years. The effect seems strongest for preventing onset rather than reversing progression once a child is already myopic.
edges.summary: The strongest evidence comes from a 2017 meta-analysis and a later cluster-randomized school trial in China. Together they show that giving children more outdoor time lowers the odds of becoming myopic, even if the size of benefit depends on how much extra time is actually achieved.
edges.caveats: The preventive signal is stronger for onset than for progression in already-myopic children. Outdoor time also travels with lower near-work burden and broader lifestyle differences, so some observational estimates may overstate the isolated effect.
